💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in New Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852.
  • The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back.
  • Recent findings suggest that “What happened this July was really special,” states George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in New Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852. Just a few months later—lightning speed in museum time—The Art Newspaper has learned that the institution has reached an agreement with Drake’s heirs to restore ownership of the work and purchase it back for its permanent collection.

The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back. Momentum built from there and return agreements were reached with institutions including the Telfair Museums in Savannah and the Georgia Museum of Art in Athens, Georgia, the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, and others.

Recent findings suggest that “What happened this July was really special,” states George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family. A letter the Newark Museum sent to the artist’s descendants and shared with The Art Newspaper states: “We acquired a jug by your ancestor in 2022 to help us more powerfully teach the history of enslavement and enslaved labour, as part of the 2023 reimagining and reinstallation of our American art galleries, Seeing America: 18th and 19th Century.” Noting the MFA Boston partnership, the museum extended the opportunity to meet and “identify ways we might collaborate”.

According to Lisa Funderburke, the Newark Museum’s director and chief executive, it was the museum’s senior director of registration and collections management, Amber Germano, who first approached her over the summer and asked if she would be willing to sign a letter.

“It’s not uncommon for curators to visit my office with a stack of papers of things that are either for consideration or ongoing engagement on articles of repatriation,” Funderburke indicates. “Always my first question is: ‘Can you articulate to me what we’re doing here and what the impulse behind that is?’”.

According to Yaba Baker, one of Drake’s fourth great-grandsons, Funderburke credited her staff with the initial action. “Lisa understood immediately what needed to be done,” Baker states. “One thing my family all agreed on: Dave is such a powerful figure in art history and Black history that to take the pots out of public view would be a disservice.”.

According to recent reports, things moved promptly after that, with additional family meetings and Funderburke’s conversations with board members and other leaders at the museum. “I felt like this would be a strong north star for our board about where we are and where we want to be, and position ourselves as a museum into the future,” the director claims.

After the museum commissioned several appraisals of the ceramic vessel, a value of around $135,000 was decided on. Numerous Drake pots have sold for five- and six-figure prices; the current record at auction for one of his works is the $1.65m paid for his 25-Gallon Poem Jar (1858), achieved at Crocker Farm Auctions in Maryland in 2021.

“Our approach is this should not be a zero-sum game,” Fatheree notes, describing the outcome in Newark as a “win-win”.

Baker concurs, stressing the enduring lessons of Drake’s legacy. “He was a slave. He was considered three fifths of a person by the US constitution,” Baker states, adding that anti-literacy laws in South Carolina at the time forbade teaching enslaved people to write.

“For our family, it’s telling the story of someone who was considered by a lot of people to be nothing, but he conducted himself with such excellence,” Baker says, before quoting a famous inscription Drake wrote on another of his vessels that begins, “I wonder where is all my relation”, and concludes: “Friendship to all.”.

Latest Update: Intolerance of Uncertainty Surged 3x Faster Since 2012

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A large-scale meta-analysi reveals that intolerance of uncertainty, a core cognitive driver of clinical anxiety, has climbed steadily among North American college students since 1992, accelerating threefold faster after 2012.
  • Source: Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.
  • Over the past decade, rates of anxiety and mood disorders among adolescents and college-aged adults have climbed sharply across North America.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A large-scale meta-analysi reveals that intolerance of uncertainty, a core cognitive driver of clinical anxiety, has climbed steadily among North American college students since 1992, accelerating threefold faster after 2012. The analysis of over 35,000 participants indicates that rising youth anxiety reflects genuine shifts in psychological distress rather than mere mental health awareness.

Source: Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

Over the past decade, rates of anxiety and mood disorders among adolescents and college-aged adults have climbed sharply across North America. Yet clinicians and epidemiologists have hotly debated a central question: does this statistical surge reflect a true rise in underlying psychological distress, or are young people simply more familiar with clinical terminology and more willing to report symptoms?

Fresh research led by Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and Boston University School of Public Health provides compelling evidence that underlying cognitive vulnerability is genuinely intensifying.

Published in JAMA Psychiatry, the study tracks three decades of data on intolerance of uncertainty (IU)—a foundational psychological mechanism characterized by acute distress when facing ambiguous situations, missing information, or unpredictable outcomes.

Analyzing data from more than 35,000 college students in the United States and Canada between 1992 and 2023, the researchers found that intolerance of uncertainty increased steadily over 30 years—and accelerated dramatically around 2012, growing roughly three times faster over the past decade than during the 1990s and 2000s.

Industry observers note that to track population-level shifts in how young adults tolerate ambiguity, first author Dr. Jeroen M. Van Baar, postdoctoral associate in epidemiology at Boston University School of Public Health, and senior author Dr. Katherine M. Keyes, professor of epidemiology at Columbia Mailman School of Public Health, conducted a systematic temporal meta-analysis using the Web of Science database.

In a recent development, after screening nearly 300 full-text peer-reviewed studies published between 2007 and 2025, the team synthesized data from 138 studies encompassing 35,296 college-aged participants across the U.S. and Canada who completed standardized 27-item or 12-item versions of the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale.

Industry observers note that across the entire 31-year window from 1992 through 2023, average IU scores increased by approximately 0.65 points annually. Crucially, the trajectory bent sharply upward around 2012: between 2012 and 2023, intolerance of uncertainty rose at roughly triple the annual pace recorded between 1992 and 2011.

“Our results provide updated insights into one of the core building blocks of anxiety: intolerance of uncertainty,” explained Keyes. “IU is not itself a health outcome or a root cause of disease, but an intermediary cognitive process that contributes to the development of anxiety.”.

For an individual with high intolerance of uncertainty, everyday unpredictability, such as attending a latest class without knowing every expectation or navigating an unstructured social event, can trigger disproportionate cognitive threat and emotional distress. Elevated IU is a well-established transdiagnostic risk factor linked to generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and depression.

Crucially, because “intolerance of uncertainty” remains a specialized clinical metric largely unfamiliar outside psychology, it provides a vital safeguard against reporting bias.

“Some researchers have argued that increases in anxiety and mood disorder symptoms among young people may partly reflect greater mental health awareness,” noted Van Baar. “Because young people are now more familiar with terms like ‘anxiety’, they may be more likely to report symptoms in surveys even if their underlying feelings have not changed. On the other hand, intolerance of uncertainty remains a relatively unfamiliar concept outside psychology, making this study less vulnerable to that criticism.”.

“The fact that we observed a consistent increase in intolerance of uncertainty that mirrored trends in anxiety and mood disorder symptoms suggests these patterns are unlikely to be explained solely by greater mental health awareness and may instead reflect genuine changes in underlying mental health,” Keyes added.

While the study did not isolate a single environmental trigger, the authors point to a convergence of mutually reinforcing societal shifts—including the rapid adoption of smartphones and social media around 2012, escalating academic competition, rising loneliness, economic instability, childhood adversity, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

“It is likely that these factors are intertwined and mutually reinforcing, jointly contributing to population-level increases in intolerance of uncertainty and anxiety among young adults,” Van Baar remarked. “Any explanation will be strongest if it accounts for both the long-term upward trend since the 1990s and the inflection point observed around 2012.”.

Sources indicate that despite the sobering trajectory, the researchers emphasize a clear path forward: unlike broad macroeconomic forces, intolerance of uncertainty is a modifiable cognitive habit. Targeted cognitive-behavioral therapies specifically designed to build tolerance for ambiguity already exist, and scaling these interventions for young adults could help curb the youth anxiety crisis at its cognitive roots.

What is “intolerance of uncertainty,” and how does it relate to anxiety?

Intolerance of uncertainty is a psychological tendency to feel distressed, overwhelmed, or threatened when facing unpredictable outcomes or missing information. It acts as a core cognitive building block that significantly increases a person’s vulnerability to developing anxiety and mood disorders.

How much has intolerance of uncertainty increased among college students?

Analyzing data from 35,296 U.S. and Canadian college students between 1992 and 2023, researchers found that scores rose steadily by about 0.65 points per year, and accelerated three times faster between 2012 and 2023 compared to the previous two decades.

Does this prove rising youth anxiety isn’t just due to greater mental health awareness?

According to recent reports, yes, it provides strong evidence against the “awareness-only” theory. Because “intolerance of uncertainty” is a specialized psychological concept rather than an everyday term young people use to self-label, its steep rise mirrors anxiety trends without being skewed by changing vocabulary or awareness.

Funding: The study was supported by the National Institute of Mental Health, grant 5T32MH013043.The authors have no financial conflicts of interest to declare.

In a recent development, intolerance of Uncertainty among U.S. and Canadian Young Adults Attending College 1992-2023: A Meta-analysis.

Sources indicate that rising anxiety prevalence among young adults may relate to intolerance of uncertainty (IU), difficulty enduring the perceived absence of vital information. A prior meta-analysis found increasing long-form Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS) scores among US and Canadian undergraduates from 1992 to 2014, but recent evidence is lacking.

To estimate IU trends among US and Canadian young adults attending college 1992-2023 by extending the prior meta-analysis and including the short-form IUS.

Web of Science was used to track English-language articles from Canada or the US citing the source articles for the long-form or short-form IUS across 13 databases.

Eligible studies were peer-reviewed empirical articles with nonclinical undergraduate samples from the US or Canada that reported sample size and mean long-form or short-form IUS.

Recent findings suggest that following MOOSE guidelines, 2 investigators extracted study characteristics and mean IU, resolving discrepancies jointly. Studies were merged with the prior meta-analysis and analyzed using fixed-effect meta-regression. To assess IU across scale forms, mean IU was converted into SD units and regressed onto data collection year, weighted by sample size, and adjusted for mean age and sex or gender distribution. Study data were analyzed from September 2025 to July 2026.

In a recent development, mean IU. The hypothesis was preregistered before data collection.

Of 799 abstracts screened and 294 full texts reviewed independently by 2 investigators, 92 articles (11%) met selection criteria. After merger with prior meta-analysis and removal of duplicates, this meta-analysis included 137 studies (62 long-form IUS and 75 short-form IUS) comprising 37 298 participants (unweighted median [IQR] of sample mean age, 20.1 [19.4-21.3] years; 69.5% female [unweighted mean of sample sex/gender distribution]). Mean long-form IU increased from 1992 to 2023 by 0.66 points annually (95% CI, 0.47-0.84 points) on a scale from 27 to 135. Mean short-form IU increased from 2005 (first sample) to 2023 by 0.60 points annually (95% CI, 0.43-0.76 points) on a scale from 12 to 60. In the combined sample, mean IU grew by 0.04 SD per year from 1992 to 2023 (95% CI, 0.03-0.05 SD per year), with 3-fold faster growth during 2012-2023 (0.06 SD per year; 95% CI, 0.04-0.08 SD per year) than during 1992-2011 (0.02 SD per year; 95% CI, 0-0.04 SD per year).

Recent findings suggest that results of this meta-analysis suggest that IU increased among US and Canadian young adults attending college 1992-2023, with a steeper increase after 2012. This supports further investigating the role of uncertainty in the epidemiology of anxiety.

#46140. This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans

📅 25 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1731 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans

📅 25 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People living thousands of miles apart have reported an extraordinarily strange experience after eating certain wild mushrooms.
  • Sources indicate that these visions are known as Lilliputian hallucinations, named after the miniature inhabitants of "Gulliver's Travels," who stand just 6 inches tall.
  • Now, a latest study provides evidence that the phenomenon has a biological explanation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People living thousands of miles apart have reported an extraordinarily strange experience after eating certain wild mushrooms. They begin seeing tiny human figures that appear to move through the real world, walking around objects, climbing over surfaces, and interacting with their surroundings.

Sources indicate that these visions are known as Lilliputian hallucinations, named after the miniature inhabitants of "Gulliver's Travels," who stand just 6 inches tall. For decades, researchers suspected that cultural beliefs and folklore might explain why people in different regions described such similar experiences.

Now, a latest study provides evidence that the phenomenon has a biological explanation.

Researchers at the University of Utah (U) used DNA sequencing to identify Lanmaoa asiatica as the mushroom responsible for these unusual hallucinations in Southwest China and the northern Philippines. Surprisingly, their investigation found no evidence of any known psychoactive mushroom compounds, including psilocybin.

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that the mushroom may produce an entirely unfamiliar hallucinogenic substance. Identifying that chemical could help scientists better understand neurological disorders, unusual visual experiences, and the processes through which the brain creates our perception of reality.

Recent findings suggest that the research was conducted by Colin Domnauer, a doctoral student at the U, and Bryn Dentinger, a mycologist affiliated with the university and the Natural History Museum of Utah. Their findings were published in the journal Mycologia.

In an interview with @theU, Domnauer explained how researchers traced the mushroom's identity, what makes its effects so unusual, and why the discovery could have implications far beyond the study of fungi.

A Century-Old Mystery of Tiny Human Hallucinations.

According to recent reports, the scientific mystery dates back to 1934, when Western researchers learned that people in Papua New Guinea sometimes experienced vivid visions of miniature humans after eating wild mushrooms. The bizarre effect became known as "mushroom madness.".

During the 1950s and 1960s, anthropologists and mushroom specialists traveled to Papua Upcoming Guinea to investigate. Their work pointed toward several possible species belonging to the Boletaceae (bolete) family.

It has been revealed that however, chemical testing failed to reveal any substances that could explain the hallucinations. Samples were even examined by Albert Hofmann, the scientist who first isolated psilocybin and discovered LSD. He, too, was unable to identify an active ingredient.

With no chemical explanation available, some researchers began questioning whether the mushrooms were responsible at all. They suggested that the visions might instead arise from cultural expectations or traditional beliefs. By the end of the 1960s, scientific investigation of the phenomenon had largely stopped.

The mystery resurfaced during the 1990s, when people in Yunnan, Southwest China, reported similar hallucinations after eating bolete mushrooms. Although the precise species remained uncertain, researchers suspected a recently described mushroom called Lanmaoa asiatica.

Scientists Identify the Mushroom Behind the Strange Visions.

Another notable clue appeared in 2024, when Domnauer learned of comparable experiences among an Indigenous community in the remote Northern Cordillera region of the Philippines.

In a recent development, community members described a wild edible mushroom called "Sedesdem" that could sometimes cause people to see miniature human figures. Similar mushrooms were known locally as "Nonda" in Papua New Guinea and "Jian shou qing" in Yunnan.

These mushrooms have an vital place in local food traditions, but consuming them without thoroughly cooking them can trigger the unusual hallucinations.

The Philippine accounts represented a third independent report of wild mushrooms causing remarkably similar visions of tiny people.

According to recent reports, to investigate, Domnauer traveled to Yunnan and the Philippines, interviewed local residents, and collected specimens of L. asiatica along with other mushrooms belonging to the Lanmaoa genus.

Industry observers note that the fieldwork included the first scientific survey of fungi in the northern Philippines. Researchers then analyzed DNA from the collected mushrooms to establish their identities and evolutionary relationships.

The results revealed that the mushrooms called Jian shou qing in China and Sedesdem in the Philippines were both L. asiatica.

This was an unexpected finding because scientists had previously believed the species occurred only in China.

Dentinger also visited Papua Fresh Guinea in hopes of collecting specimens from the location where the mystery originally began. Unfortunately, unusually dry weather made it impossible to obtain samples for genetic comparison.

Sources indicate that although the Papua New Guinea mushroom remains unverified, the evidence from China and the Philippines provides a compelling connection. Three geographically separated cultures have described the same highly specific hallucinations, and DNA testing has linked two of those cases to a single mushroom species.

That consistency strongly suggests a shared chemical and neurological explanation rather than unrelated cultural influences.

Hallucinations of Tiny Humans That Seem Remarkably Real.

What makes these hallucinations especially unusual is their striking similarity across different accounts.

People typically describe seeing dozens or even hundreds of miniature figures, generally measuring between 3 and 30 centimeters tall. The figures appear with extraordinary clarity, often seeming as solid and convincing as actual people.

According to Domnauer, approximately 90% of those experiencing the visions describe figures resembling elves, clowns, or other fairy-like characters, often wearing brightly colored clothing.

Even more surprising is the way these imaginary figures seem to behave.

Rather than floating through walls or ignoring their surroundings, they appear to follow familiar physical rules. They walk around obstacles, move across ordinary objects, and sometimes tumble from the edges of tables.

Domnauer recalled one particularly unusual account involving someone eating soup. The person reported seeing tiny humans leap from a spoon into the bowl, where they began swimming. When the person took another spoonful, the miniature figures reportedly remained visible inside their mouth.

Such detailed interactions distinguish these visions from many other forms of drug-induced hallucination.

A Mysterious Psychedelic Compound Unlike Any Known Drug.

Industry observers note that scientists also investigated whether L. asiatica contains any of the chemicals already known to cause psychedelic experiences.

Using both chemical testing and genetic analysis, the researchers searched for established psychoactive compounds found in other mushroom species.

The absence of familiar hallucinogens was particularly intriguing because the mushroom's effects differ so dramatically from those associated with known psychedelic drugs.

Sources indicate that researchers now suspect that L. asiatica produces an unidentified psychoactive substance responsible for the tiny human hallucinations.

The compound has not yet been isolated or chemically identified, so its exact nature and mechanism remain unknown.

Discovering it could open an entirely new avenue of research into how certain chemicals alter visual perception.

What the Mushroom Could Reveal About the Human Brain.

It has been revealed that although L. asiatica provides an unusually consistent trigger for Lilliputian hallucinations, the phenomenon is not limited to mushroom consumption.

It has been revealed that stories involving miniature humanlike beings appear throughout folklore around the world. Similar hallucinations have also been documented in people experiencing alcohol withdrawal, dementia, macular degeneration, and other neurological conditions.

These connections suggest that the visions may arise from a fundamental feature of the way the human brain processes visual information.

However, scientists still do not fully understand the neurological mechanisms responsible for these experiences or how best to treat them when they occur in medical settings.

This is where the mysterious mushroom could become especially valuable.

Sources indicate that unlike the neurological and medical conditions in which Lilliputian hallucinations occur relatively rarely, L. asiatica can produce the phenomenon in a more consistent and recognizable way.

If researchers can isolate the chemical responsible, they may gain a useful tool for investigating the brain circuits and processes that create these unusually detailed visual experiences.

Such research could eventually improve scientific understanding of hallucinations associated with neurological diseases.

The research team's next major objective is to isolate and identify the suspected psychedelic compound.

DNA Sequencing Reveals Four Previously Unknown Mushroom Species.

The investigation also produced important discoveries about fungal biodiversity.

Rather than studying L. asiatica alone, Domnauer and Dentinger conducted the first comprehensive genomic analysis of the Lanmaoa genus.

They examined 53 mushroom specimens collected from natural habitats and preserved in fungarium collections around the world.

Genetic sequencing revealed 17 species within the group, including four species previously unknown to science.

According to recent reports, remarkably, two of those newly identified species had already been preserved in existing collections in the United States. Their distinct identities had gone unrecognized until researchers examined their DNA.

The analysis also indicated that L. asiatica is the only species in the genus currently known to produce psychoactive effects.

Recent findings suggest that scientists are now working to reconstruct the group's evolutionary history. They hope to determine how the unusual chemical trait developed and whether closely related mushrooms might produce comparable substances.

Recent findings suggest that the findings also demonstrate the scientific value of museum collections. Specimens preserved for years can contain biological discoveries that become apparent only when newer analytical techniques are applied.

For Domnauer, the hidden diversity found in these collections is a reminder that many species and potentially important biological characteristics remain undiscovered, even among organisms that scientists have already collected.

Exploring Fungi Could Lead to New Medicines and Discoveries.

The broader implications extend well beyond unusual hallucinations.

Fungi remain one of the least thoroughly explored groups of organisms, and researchers believe their chemical diversity could provide valuable clues about biology, medicine, and the nervous system.

One of the most famous examples is penicillin, the antibiotic originally obtained from a fungus that transformed the treatment of bacterial infections and became one of the most consequential medical discoveries of the last century.

Scientists hope continued exploration of fungal biodiversity could reveal other medically useful compounds and previously unknown biological processes.

The mysterious effects of L. asiatica illustrate just how much remains to be learned about the fungal kingdom. A mushroom long consumed by communities in Asia may contain a substance capable of revealing upcoming information about the human brain and how it creates conscious experience.

For How Long Do You Need to Meditate?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picture this: 71 adults signed up for a study comparing brief to longer mindfulness practice.
  • Participants were divided at random into three groups: One group got 20 minutes of mindfulness meditation, a second group got five minutes, and the control group relaxed with audiobook excerpts from Bill Bryson’s A Short History of Nearly Everything, Bryson’s soothing recounting of the cosmos and our place in it.
  • In studies like these, “mindfulness meditation” typically means sitting quietly, eyes closed or softened, resting nonjudgmental attention on your breath or bodily sensations, gently noticing when your mind wanders (as it will), and just as gently bringing it back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture this: 71 adults signed up for a study comparing brief to longer mindfulness practice. Many had never meditated, while others had dabbled years before.

Participants were divided at random into three groups: One group got 20 minutes of mindfulness meditation, a second group got five minutes, and the control group relaxed with audiobook excerpts from Bill Bryson’s A Short History of Nearly Everything, Bryson’s soothing recounting of the cosmos and our place in it.

In studies like these, “mindfulness meditation” typically means sitting quietly, eyes closed or softened, resting nonjudgmental attention on your breath or bodily sensations, gently noticing when your mind wanders (as it will), and just as gently bringing it back.

Now, you might expect that longer meditations would deliver greater benefits. After all, we’re conditioned to believe that more is better—especially when it comes to self-improvement. But this research and many other studies find that more minutes don’t necessarily mean more benefit: Shorter practices can work just as well—and sometimes better—while consistency may matter more than duration.

Industry observers note that in this first study, each participant attended four 25-minute sessions over two weeks. In every session, the time not spent on audio-guided mindfulness-of-breath practice was filled by Bryson’s eloquence. To ensure the results reflected only the study activities, participants were asked to avoid any formal mindfulness practices outside these sessions.

After those two weeks, the five-minute meditators actually revealed greater improvements in stress and mindful awareness (the tendency to stay present in daily life with less judgement) than the 20-minute group. Even depression and anxiety improved just as much—if not more.

Was the extra time with Bryson the magic ingredient for those five-minute meditators? The control group, who luxuriated in 25 uninterrupted minutes of his charm, highlighted no meaningful improvement. So while his voice may soothe, it wasn’t what moved the needle.

One five-minute meditator put it this way: “I always thought that to do mindfulness, I’d need a long time to dedicate to this, which seemed too challenging to even start. But I’ve learned that five minutes can help!” In contrast, a 20-minute participant admitted, “I think a shorter one would be better for me to learn mindfulness.”.

There’s more. The facilitator observed that participants in the 20-minute meditation sessions more often fidgeted, shifted in their seats, and peeked through half-closed eyes, as if tranquility were just out of reach. Meanwhile, the five-minute meditators appeared more at ease and less prone to these signs of discomfort. Five of them even requested recordings to continue at home. The 20-minute group? Not a single request. For these beginners, less really did seem to be more.

Now, before you dash off to cancel that meditation retreat, remember that this study focused on people with little to no meditation experience. So if you’re a seasoned meditator, those longer sessions might still pack more punch for you, as we’ll explore later. And both the five-minute and 20-minute groups indicated improvements in mindful awareness, depression, anxiety, and stress compared to the control group. The five-minute meditators just improved more when it came to mindful awareness and stress.

In a recent development, the takeaway? For beginners, a quick dip into mindfulness might be more refreshing than a long soak.

You might be wondering, Isn’t this just one study? Could it be a fluke? But multiple randomized controlled trials have explored how the length of meditation shapes its impact.

I join Christine Carter, Ph.D, in a webinar next week to talk about my book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick.

In a recent development, in the largest of these studies, researchers recruited 372 adults online—about half of them newly introduced to meditation—to see how the “dose” of mindfulness meditation affected mindful awareness and emotional well-being. Participants were randomly sorted into one of four groups: Some meditated for 10 minutes, others for 20, and the rest listened to a 10- or 20-minute National Geographic article on sequoia trees. (Because nothing soothes stress like a deep dive into bark thickness.).

In a recent development, what did the researchers find? The 10-minute meditators indicated greater improvements in mindful awareness than those who listened to the 10-minute sequoia lecture. Surprisingly, the 20-minute meditation group didn’t outperform any group—not even the tree enthusiasts. In fact, the 10-minute group showed slightly greater improvements in mindful awareness than the 20-minute meditators, although the difference wasn’t statistically significant, meaning it could have occurred by chance. Still, it suggests that for boosting mindful awareness right after practice, 10 minutes might be at least as effective as 20.

According to recent reports, but that was just one session. What happens with consistent practice? In another study, 77 college students were randomly assigned to meditate daily for 10 or 20 minutes. After two weeks, both groups indicated similar improvements in stress and, again, mindful awareness. But those assigned to the 20-minute group experienced a slightly greater boost in self-compassion, the skill of meeting your own struggles with the kindness you’d offer a dear friend.

In a recent development, so if you’ve poured hours into longer meditations, you can rest easy—it wasn’t for nothing. The evidence suggests that whether your sessions are short or sustained, they can offer meaningful benefits.

Another notable finding is that the 10-minute group practiced more consistently, logging about 82 minutes total. The 20-minute group missed more days and didn’t always finish, ending up with just 103. Double the goal, barely a quarter more practice.

If you’ve ever tried meditating, you might be nodding along. Some sessions are bliss, while others are a tug-of-war with time. Maybe you’ve battled that nagging frustration, trying to keep your mind steady for more than a fleeting moment. Or felt the magnetic pull of distraction, your mind wandering just when you need it to stay put. As the minutes crawl, doubt can creep in: Am I even doing this right? Is it worth it? These tough moments can teach you a lot, but they can also make meditation feel intimidating—and make you less likely to stick with it, especially when you’re just starting out. Another study looked at even longer sessions, comparing 10 minutes of meditation to 30 minutes. This experiment split 161 adults into four groups: 10 or 30 minutes of daily sitting meditation, or the same amount of mindful movement. The mindful movement was a stretching practice that brings mindful awareness into motion—less stillness, same presence.

After two weeks, everyone saw benefits: Mindful awareness increased, well-being improved, and distress levels dropped. But there were no significant differences among the groups. Whether they meditated for 10 minutes or 30, sitting or moving, all the groups seemed to benefit equally.

So, here’s the bottom line: One study found that longer sessions more strongly boosted self-compassion. Another indicated that shorter ones more effectively reduced stress. But across studies, most of the key benefits—mindful awareness, mental health, well-being—weren’t tied to how long people practiced.

Why? Because as we’ll keep exploring, the nervous system learns through repetition, not duration. It’s consistency that reshapes patterns. Not heroic efforts once in a while, but showing up, again and again, however you can.

In a recent development, the benefits of consistency over length show up in observational studies, too, where people choose how often and how long to meditate. While observational studies can’t pin down cause and effect, they offer a richer view of how shorter practices play out in the real world.

Industry observers note that imagine it’s early morning. You reach for your phone and open Insight Timer, a free meditation app. Before your meditation, it asks, “How are you today?” You tap an icon—maybe “OK,” maybe “great”—capturing a snapshot of your mood in seconds.

Now imagine doing this regularly, for 14 months straight. That’s exactly what 10,409 people from 103 countries did in a groundbreaking study. Many were upcoming to meditation, using the app to track their emotional ups and downs in real time. It’s like taking your emotional temperature—not with a thermometer, but with a single tap that sums up how you feel.

The findings? Consistency (four to seven days a week)—not duration—was the strongest predictor of better mood, resilience, and equanimity, the ability to stay cool under pressure. Think of it like watering a plant: A little each week keeps it happy and growing. Forget all month and drown it after four weeks? It wilts anyway.

For beginners in the Insight Timer study, short sessions—five to 10 minutes—outshone longer ones in improving mood over time. But after 20 sessions? Longer practices—21 to 30 minutes—began to take the lead in mood improvement. It’s like your brain needs to build its meditation muscles before longer sessions feel better than short ones—like a marathon that only gives you the high once you’ve earned it.

But do shorter sessions lose their impact as you gain experience? Not at all. They might just become your secret weapon. After 80 sessions, shorter practices make a late-game comeback, boosting equanimity and showing that even seasoned meditators can benefit from briefer sessions.

Industry observers note that the idea that consistency beats duration is backed by a meta-analysis challenging the belief that longer equals better. Think of a meta-analysis as a “study of studies,” combining data from multiple research papers to uncover clearer, big-picture insights.

When researchers analyzed 203 randomized controlled trials totaling 15,971 participants, they found no association between meditation session length and better outcomes. In fact, a trend emerged in favor of shorter practices for reducing depression symptoms, although it wasn’t statistically significant. Still, shorter sessions were at least as effective as longer ones, calling into question the assumption that more minutes always mean more benefits. So what’s the takeaway? When you’re starting out, don’t sweat the long stuff. Quick sessions might do more to lift your mood early on. As you settle in, longer practices might bring deeper emotional gains. But even if you’re a pro, short sessions don’t lose their value—they just shift their superpower, helping you stay steady when life throws you curveballs. Different strengths, different stages. And who doesn’t love a shortcut that actually works?

Eli Susman, Ph.D., is a UC Berkeley-trained psychologist, former Harvard researcher, and author of Micropractice: A Science-Backed Approach for Calm, Clarity, and Joy in 30 Seconds or Less, forthcoming in 22 languages.

#46138. Losing a Single “Molecular Brake” Gene Triggers Brain Overgrowth

Losing a Single “Molecular Brake” Gene Triggers Brain Overgrowth

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, researchers mapped the cellular domino effect triggered when developing brain stem cells lose the Pten gene.
  • Source: Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) / Science Advances.
  • Building a functional human cerebral cortex requires extraordinary cellular precision: neural stem cells must divide, differentiate, and stop growing on a strict developmental schedule so that billions of neurons and glial cells assemble in exact proportions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, researchers mapped the cellular domino effect triggered when developing brain stem cells lose the Pten gene. The single-cell lineage-tracing study reveals that individual neural progenitors lacking Pten generate 25% more neurons alongside an excess of enlarged astrocytes, and reroute glial cell production through the MAPK pathway, offering a potential new target for drug-resistant brain tumors.

Source: Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) / Science Advances.

Building a functional human cerebral cortex requires extraordinary cellular precision: neural stem cells must divide, differentiate, and stop growing on a strict developmental schedule so that billions of neurons and glial cells assemble in exact proportions.

Acting as a vital molecular brake during this process is the Pten gene, which restrains cell division and keeps tissue growth balanced.

Sources indicate that when mutations disable PTEN, that biological brake fails. Individuals carrying PTEN mutations frequently develop megalencephaly, an unusually enlarged brain, alongside elevated rates of autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, epilepsy, and brain tumors, a constellation of symptoms known clinically as PTEN Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome.

Now, in a study published in Science Advances, the Hippenmeyer group at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA), collaborating with researchers at Sorbonne Université in Paris, Yale School of Medicine, and Vetmeduni Vienna, has traced the exact single-cell chain reaction unleashed when Pten is lost in developing brain stem cells.

Because switching off Pten across the entire brain causes severe early lethality in animal models, isolating how the mutation alters individual stem cell behavior has historically been difficult.

Recent findings suggest that to overcome this hurdle, first author Dr. Osvaldo Miranda Romero, a postdoctoral researcher in Simon Hippenmeyer’s laboratory at ISTA, utilized Mosaic Analysis with Double Markers (MADM), a high-precision genetic lineage-tracing technique that deletes Pten in only a tiny, sparse fraction of cortical radial glial stem cells while tagging them and all their descendants with bright fluorescent markers.

“Until now, we lacked basic information about what Pten mutations mean at the level of individual cells and how they affect cellular output, in other words, the quantity and identity of cells produced from stem cells,” explained Romero.

Tracking these fluorescent cellular family trees across mouse brain development revealed a twofold driver of brain overgrowth:.

In a recent development, to uncover how Pten loss forces stem cells to overproduce astrocytes, the team investigated the intracellular signaling pathways governing glial differentiation. Under typical developmental conditions, radial glial progenitors depend on the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) pathway to transition into astrocytes.

Sources indicate that however, when Romero and colleagues simultaneously switched off both Pten and Egfr in individual radial glial cells, astrocyte overproduction continued unabated. Molecular analysis revealed that Pten-deficient progenitors had completely bypassed the standard EGFR route, rerouting glial differentiation through an alternative signaling cascade: the MAPK pathway.

“Under normal conditions, EGFR is an important driver of glial-cell formation, whereas MAPK can serve as a kind of alternative route under exceptional circumstances,” Romero noted.

Industry observers note that beyond illuminating the developmental origins of autism and megalencephaly, this signaling detour carries direct implications for neuro-oncology. Patients with PTEN mutations face a heightened risk of developing gliomas, aggressive brain tumors composed of astrocytes and other glial cells.

Sources indicate that clinicians frequently treat gliomas with drugs designed to block EGFR signaling, yet many patients eventually develop treatment resistance. By demonstrating that Pten loss allows glial cells to sidestep EGFR via MAPK activation, the study highlights a promising therapeutic target.

“Our findings suggest that the MAPK signaling pathway could be investigated as a potential therapeutic target in such cases in the future,” Romero concluded.

How does losing the Pten gene lead to an unusually large brain (megalencephaly)?

Researchers at ISTA found that when individual brain stem cells (radial glia) lack the Pten gene, they lose their natural growth brake, producing about 25% more neurons and significantly more astrocytes than normal. Both the neurons and astrocytes also grow abnormally large, expanding overall brain tissue volume.

What conditions are linked to PTEN mutations in humans?

Mutations in PTEN are associated with PTEN Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome, which increases the likelihood of megalencephaly (enlarged brain size), autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, epilepsy, and glial brain tumors called gliomas.

How could this discovery help treat brain tumors in the future?

Glial brain tumors are often treated with drugs that block the EGFR signaling pathway, but tumors frequently become resistant. Researchers discovered that cells missing Pten bypass EGFR by switching to the alternative MAPK pathway to make astrocytes—suggesting that targeting MAPK could help overcome drug resistance.

Pten Regulates Neurogenic Radial Glia Lineage Progression and Tunes Neocortical Astrocyte Production in Mapk1/3-dependent Pathway.

Recent findings suggest that the cerebral cortex consists of immense numbers of diverse cell types derived from radial glial progenitor (RGP) cells. How RGPs generate appropriate quantities of distinct cell types to safeguard a brain of correct size is not well understood. However, genetic aberrations in human, including mutations in PTEN, lead to cortical malformation such as macrocephaly, albeit with unknown etiology.

Here, we used mosaic analysis with double markers (MADM)–based clonal analysis and single-cell phenotyping to decipher the role of Pten in RGP lineage progression during cortical ontogeny. Although neurogenic RGP lineage progression was altered and projection neuron production doubled in the absence of Pten, cortical astrogenesis was drastically increased. Through epistasis experiments, we show that the loss of Pten uncouples astrogenesis from essential growth factor signaling hubs, funneling into MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase).

Collectively, our results suggest that Pten regulates RGP lineage progression with distinct sequential functions in corticogenesis to safeguard the emergence of a correctly sized cortex.

#46136. How to Make Better Decisions in the Age of AI

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2082 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

How to Make Better Decisions in the Age of AI

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that artificial intelligence can summarize research, generate ideas, and analyze enormous amounts of data in seconds.
  • Sources indicate that AI has the power to enhance decision-making—or to overwhelm it.
  • In a recent development, she argues that the rise of AI actually makes certain human qualities like reflection, empathy, values, and moral judgment even more important.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence can summarize research, generate ideas, and analyze enormous amounts of data in seconds. The power of that little “Ask anything” AI prompt box is immense, but can it help us make wiser decisions? Cheryl Strauss Einhorn, author of The Human Edge: Smarter Decisions in the Age of AI, writes:.

Sources indicate that AI has the power to enhance decision-making—or to overwhelm it. It can illuminate pathways we might not have seen or narrow our choices in ways we do not fully recognize. As AI systems become more integrated into our lives, the challenge is no longer simply about harnessing their power but about leading them with clarity, discernment, and commitment to human agency.

In a recent development, she argues that the rise of AI actually makes certain human qualities like reflection, empathy, values, and moral judgment even more important. We spoke with her about why human judgment is a competitive advantage, how to engage our values when we prompt AI, and how AI can help us clarify our thinking.

Kia Afcari: You argue that AI makes human judgment more, not less, important. How can we make sure that the values of kindness and care are reflected when we use AI to help us make decisions?

Cheryl Strauss Einhorn: AI has no values. It has biases and influences by those who have designed it, and from whatever information has been fed into it. So to be sure that prosocial values are reflected when we use AI, we humans need to bring them into the work that we do together.

Recent findings suggest that when working with an AI tool, we want to be asking ourselves, What is the problem that I’m solving? Why am I solving it? What is the context? And so we really need to be intentional with AI, because without asking ourselves those things first, AI doesn’t know why we’re coming to it.

Before you actually sit down with a tool, you can muster those values and those crucial factors related to the problem that you’re solving, and then articulate them and communicate them to the machine.

If we let the machine think for us, we can lose that sense of right and wrong, for example, because we actually care about all of those details that AI can’t possibly know about the problems that we’re solving and the people that we’re solving those problems with and for.

For example, you might ask yourself or your AI tool: Before I act, help me think through the people, relationships, and responsibilities this decision affects—not just the outcome it produces.

This type of human-centric AI interaction helped Felice, a food scientist at a pet food tech giant, who was responsible for developing latest recipes that balance nutrition, taste, and market trends. She often has to delegate tasks within her research team, ensuring that product testing, ingredient sourcing, and regulatory compliance all move forward smoothly. Using AI, she was able to analyze workloads and expertise that suggested the best person for each task, but only Felice understood the deeper dynamics at play—who works best under tight deadlines, who has a passion for innovative formulations, and who needs mentorship. When AI recommended assigning a crucial stability test to her most experienced technician, this prompt supported her thinking about a different option: giving it to the junior scientist who was eager to develop his skills in quality assurance. The AI tool’s choices made sense based on efficiency, but Felice’s decision ensured both short-term success and long-term team development.

Industry observers note that KA: In the book, your “cheetah” metaphor celebrates slowing down. Why is a strategic pause so vital when working with AI?

In a recent development, CSE: The cheetah metaphor relates that although this is an animal that goes zero to 60 in about three seconds, its hunting prowess actually comes from being able to decelerate up to nine miles an hour in a single stride. And the reason why that’s so important in problem solving and decision making is that’s where you build agility, flexibility, and maneuverability. Do I want to stay the course, or do I want to pivot and do something else?

This pause allows you to chunk your learning and pry open that cognitive space for newly introduced information and insight. With an AI tool, it’s so important because there’s a difference between speed and quality.

When something truly matters to us, we want to make sure that we’re solving the problem in a way that solves it holistically, that takes care of the people who are involved in the problem with us. And when we’re moving really promptly, sometimes those very important factors are hard to bring forward. So there’s a real difference between what is efficient and what is effective.

KA: Why can having more information make it harder—not easier—to make good decisions?

CSE: Francis Bacon once said, “Knowledge is power,” but that’s not really true anymore, right? We now have all of the answers with AI to a lot of commonly asked questions and some uncommon questions.

It has been revealed that we need to make sure we’re defining the problem that we’re solving, that we are understanding and communicating the motivation and providing the context, because you don’t want all the information. Otherwise, we’re going to end up with analysis paralysis.

One thing people can use is what I call the “vision of success” question. This question asks you to time travel, to jump over the decision to see that the decision has been made well. What’s happening? What are those few things that if they don’t succeed, the decision fails? It’s actually very powerful, because it allows you to clearly identify so that you can articulate those factors that you absolutely need to be able to share with AI. These become the constraints and boundaries that set the perimeter around the decision, so that it can give you research that’s targeted and focused on those things.

For example, Max deciding where to spend his next vacation. Asking AI for help directly—without turning to himself first—he got a list of destinations, airline options, and local attractions, complete with ratings, reviews, and price comparisons. On paper, that sounds ideal. But in reality, Max quickly found himself paralyzed by the sheer amount of information. What if he picked a less-than-perfect hotel? What if he overlooked a hidden gem? AI has handed him a mountain of data, but it didn’t necessarily make the decision any easier.

However, when he used the “vision of success” question, he was able to realize and to share with his AI tool: “I want to return home feeling genuinely rested, having spent quality time with my family, without overspending or feeling like I missed the experience I was hoping for.”.

Recent findings suggest that only then does AI have a meaningful problem to solve. Instead of searching for the “best” vacation—a question with no objective answer—it can help Max find the destination most likely to produce the outcome he actually wants. AI can’t define success but it can optimize for the success you define.

KA: How does the AREA method help people make wiser decisions, especially when AI is involved? CSE: AREA is more than an acronym—it’s a framework for challenging our assumptions and thinking mistakes, and actively includes the perspectives of others. It stands for Absolute, Relative, Exploration and Exploitation, and Analysis.

Sources indicate that the first “A,” Absolute, focuses on primary, unfiltered information straight from primary sources. “R,” Relative, shifts to external viewpoints—secondary sources connected to the subject. “E,” Exploration and Exploitation, fuels creativity: Exploration broadens research through interviews and unconventional sources, while Exploitation turns inward, challenging personal biases and assumptions. The final “A,” Analysis, synthesizes everything, bringing clarity and structure to complex decisions.

Sources indicate that when using AI, a system like AREA becomes even more important because AI doesn’t eliminate bias—it can reflect and sometimes amplify biases in its training data, design, and the way we use it. Good decisions require a process that helps us recognize and challenge both AI’s biases and our own.

For AI, so much of the information, for example, is from Reddit. Information can be incomplete or outdated, and you also know that you’re interacting with a liar. It’s a machine that just gives you answers that are wrong sometimes.

So you need to be able to have a quality due diligence process to not only be able to use the tool effectively, but to be able to evaluate its outcome. Too often, people look at an answer with AI and think that it’s a transaction, and they can just take it. AREA is going to help you make sure that it’s a conversation. So you have an evidence-based perspective that has looked at a variety of stakeholder viewpoints, and made sure that you have pried open that cognitive space to challenge the natural, well-worn mental pathways that we all lean on every day.

KA: How can we use AI in ways that strengthen—rather than undermine—our values and agency?

CSE: It’s a great question. I think the upcoming competitive advantage is going to be self-awareness.

This is the first tool that actually asks for some of our cognitive load; it wants us to offload some of our decisions to it. And this is a machine fundamentally about decision making, because we ask it for something and it gives us an answer. But there’s a very interesting invitation here, which is to each of us to get to know ourselves better.

In a recent development, we each have a special sauce, which is the way that we make our decisions, and we make thousands of them every single day. But most of us have not sat down and remarked to themselves, What does that process actually look like? Can I actually name those pieces and put language to it?

There is this invitation to get to know our thinking so that we can translate it better, and not only for the tool. How helpful would it be in conversation with our colleagues to be able to say clearly, This is how I’m actually going through the steps, this is how I’m thinking about it, these are the variables that I’m prioritizing, and here’s what I think is the most diagnostic.

According to recent reports, you can think about your thinking skills as muscles. If we turn over our cognitive load, we will also weaken it. But if we actually take this invitation to understand our self-awareness and our metacognition, we can make sure that we strengthen those tools.

AI is a tool that has so many implications for our environment and for our world, in addition to the fact that it has implications for our actual thinking skills.

So I would say that the invitation is to turn to yourself first. Ask yourself why you’re using the tool, and whether or not you should be turning to yourself instead. And either way, bring your own thinking forward before sitting down, so that you can feel far more comfortable that you can problem-solve both with it and beyond it.

Screen Time and Fitness Reshape Grey Matter in Teen Brains

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A neuroimaging study reveals that daily screen time, physical activity, and physical fitness leave distinct structural signatures on the developing adolescent brain.
  • According to recent reports, adolescence is a period of profound structural remodeling in the human brain.
  • At the same time, modern teenagers navigate unprecedented daily exposure to smartphones, gaming, and digital media alongside wide variations in physical exercise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A neuroimaging study reveals that daily screen time, physical activity, and physical fitness leave distinct structural signatures on the developing adolescent brain. Using MRI scans of teenagers aged 16 to 19, researchers found that heavy smart-device usage is associated with reduced grey matter volume in memory-related medial temporal regions alongside altered maturation patterns in frontal and visual cortices.

Source: University of Eastern Finland.

According to recent reports, adolescence is a period of profound structural remodeling in the human brain. Throughout the late teenage years, neural circuits undergo a natural fine-tuning process known as synaptic pruning—trimming away redundant connections to streamline communication, boost processing efficiency, and sharpen executive control.

At the same time, modern teenagers navigate unprecedented daily exposure to smartphones, gaming, and digital media alongside wide variations in physical exercise.

In a neuroimaging investigation conducted at the University of Eastern Finland and Kuopio University Hospital, researchers examined how these everyday lifestyle factors correspond to physical differences in adolescent brain structure.

Led by Doctoral Researcher Hannamari Skog of the Institute of Biomedicine, the study evaluated 44 healthy adolescents aged 16 to 19 (25 girls and 19 boys) drawn from the Physical Activity and Nutrition in Children (PANIC) study and the FitBrain cohort.

Using high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to quantify regional grey matter volume alongside validated lifestyle questionnaires and physical fitness testing (including 50-meter shuttle runs and standing long jumps), the researchers uncovered distinct anatomical patterns tied to digital media habits:.

“Excessive screen time and smart device usage may be harmful to the areas of the brain that are involved in memory and learning,” explained Skog.

However, Skog noted that larger grey matter volume in visual and executive regions during late adolescence is not necessarily advantageous. Because typical teenage brain maturation involves a healthy reduction in grey matter as neural circuits specialize and become more efficient, persistent volume increases in frontal and occipital areas could signal either intensive visual-motor stimulation from apps and games or a developmental delay in cortical pruning.

It has been revealed that “The larger volume in these areas may be particularly related to applications and games that require attention, motor planning and visual information processing,” Skog said. “During normal brain development in adolescence, there is a reduction in grey matter volume and an increase in brain efficiency. The positive link between screen time and the volume of grey matter in these areas may thus also reflect a delay in brain development.”.

Movement and cardiovascular-muscular fitness were also reflected across multiple cortical and subcortical regions:.

Because the study relied on a cross-sectional snapshot of 44 adolescents, the authors emphasize that causal relationships and long-term cognitive outcomes require longitudinal follow-up across adulthood.

“The results provide latest information on how everyday lifestyle factors, such as screen time, physical activity and physical fitness, are linked to brain structure in adolescence,” Skog concluded. “However, in light of the results, the connections between lifestyle factors and brain structures in adolescence are complex, and more research is needed to understand their long-term significance.”.

How does heavy screen time affect the teenage brain’s structure?

MRI scans from the University of Eastern Finland show that adolescents with high leisure screen time have smaller grey matter volumes in the medial temporal lobe (critical for memory and learning), alongside larger grey matter volumes in frontal and visual regions, which may reflect either heavy visual-motor gaming demands or a delay in normal adolescent brain pruning.

Why can larger grey matter volume in teenagers sometimes indicate delayed brain development?

Recent findings suggest that during healthy adolescence, the brain naturally trims away excess grey matter through synaptic pruning to become faster and more efficient. Having unusually large grey matter volumes in frontal decision-making areas during late adolescence can therefore indicate that this natural maturational streamlining is running behind schedule.

How did physical activity and fitness affect brain volume in this study?

Higher overall physical activity was linked to larger volume in the right visual (occipital) cortex, while better physical fitness scores were associated with larger parietal lobe volume (involved in attention and spatial perception) and smaller volumes in the hippocampus and posterior cingulate gyrus.

Associations of screen time, physical activity and neuromuscular fitness with brain structure in adolescents.

To explore the associations of total screen time, smart device use, physical activity, and neuromuscular fitness with brain gray matter volumes in adolescence.

Brain gray matter volumes were assessed using magnetic resonance imaging in 44 healthy adolescents (25 females and 19 males) aged 16–19 years. Physical activity and sedentary behavior questionnaires were used to assess screen time, including smart device use, and physical activity, including organized sports in sports clubs. Neuromuscular fitness was assessed using a score combining results of a 50-m shuttle-run test and a standing long jump test.

Screen time and smart device use were negatively associated with medial temporal lobe volumes but positively associated with supplementary motor cortex and dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex volumes. Screen time was also positively related to left cuneus volume. Total physical activity was positively associated with right inferior occipital gyrus volume, but the association did not remain statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. Neuromuscular fitness was positively associated with parietal lobe volumes but negatively associated with right hippocampus and left posterior cingulate gyrus volumes, but these associations were no longer statistically significant after correction for multiple testing.

Sources indicate that longer screen time was related to lower medial temporal lobe volumes and larger frontal lobe volumes, whereas higher physical activity and better neuromuscular fitness were associated with larger volumes in the parietal and occipital regions. These findings highlight the complex relationships of screen time and physical activity with brain gray matter volumes in adolescence.

The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A major latest study has uncovered important differences in how the brains of autistic children respond to human faces.
  • Some autistic people tend to look at faces less frequently or make less eye contact.
  • James McPartland, PhD, Harris Professor in the Child Study Center and director of the Center for Brain and Mind Health, studies how autistic people process faces using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A major latest study has uncovered important differences in how the brains of autistic children respond to human faces. Published in Nature Mental Health, the research is among the most extensive investigations yet into how face perception works in autism.

Some autistic people tend to look at faces less frequently or make less eye contact. They may also find it more difficult to remember faces or interpret facial expressions compared with neurotypical individuals. Scientists have spent decades investigating the brain activity behind these differences. In the early 2000s, for example, researchers at Yale reported that brain regions responsible for processing faces showed lower activity in autistic individuals than in people without autism.

James McPartland, PhD, Harris Professor in the Child Study Center and director of the Center for Brain and Mind Health, studies how autistic people process faces using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity. Previous EEG studies, however, have typically examined signals from limited regions rather than analyzing activity across the entire scalp.

In a recent development, to gain a more complete picture, McPartland and his colleagues conducted a study involving approximately 400 autistic children, examining electrical signals recorded across the scalp. They discovered that brain activity associated with face recognition was less clearly distinguishable in autistic participants. They also identified a striking difference in development: In neurotypical children, the brain's response to faces became more specialized with age, while autistic children did not show the same pattern.

"This is the first time we've leveraged the full volume of very rich information provided by an EEG recording to understand face perception and autism," McPartland says.

How Scientists Discovered Differences in Autistic Brain Activity.

McPartland compares traditional approaches to studying face recognition with attempting to understand traffic throughout an entire city by monitoring just one downtown street.

"That's the way most research on face processing so far has worked," McPartland claims.

The latest approach provides a much broader perspective, similar to observing traffic across an entire city using satellite imagery. To investigate these patterns, the researchers analyzed information collected through the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT). The dataset included autistic and neurotypical children across different age groups.

During the experiments, participants viewed pictures of faces and everyday objects while EEG equipment recorded their brain activity. Instead of concentrating on a small number of recording locations, the scientists examined electrical signals from all 128 electrodes positioned around each participant's scalp.

They then applied machine learning techniques to determine whether patterns in the recordings could reveal what each child was viewing.

The results revealed that brain activity provided a clearer indication of face viewing in neurotypical children than in autistic children. In other words, the electrical signals associated with seeing faces were less distinguishable in the autistic group.

Sources indicate that "The neural activity that we measure at the scalp is just not as distinct in autistic children," says first author Jason Griffin, PhD, assistant professor of psychology at University of Houston. Griffin previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in McPartland's laboratory.

In a recent development, the researchers also found that the ability to identify what a child was viewing from brain activity improved with age among neurotypical participants. This age related improvement was not observed in autistic children, suggesting that their neural responses to faces develop along a different pattern.

"Their face-specific processing is not following the same trajectory," Griffin says.

Face Recognition Differences May Begin Earlier Than Previously Thought.

Beyond identifying differences in brain activity, the study offers newly introduced insight into how early those differences emerge during face perception.

Industry observers note that recognizing someone involves multiple stages of neural processing. The sequence begins when visual information enters the eyes and continues as the brain interprets that information until a face is recognized.

In a recent development, much of the earlier research on autism and face perception has concentrated on a brain signal called the N170. This measurable change in electrical activity typically occurs about 170 milliseconds after a person sees a face. Previous studies have shown that the N170 response tends to occur later in autistic individuals.

By analyzing brain activity over a wider period, the researchers found evidence that differences in face processing begin before this familiar signal appears. This suggests that autism related differences may arise at earlier stages of visual processing than researchers had previously established.

"But when you look at face processing through an approach that's more inclusive of the full temporal range of information, we're seeing that differences in autism occur even earlier," McPartland indicates.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Autism Diagnosis and Early Support.

The findings could eventually influence how researchers approach autism diagnosis and the development of supportive interventions.

Historically, some clinicians attempted to address difficulties with face perception by requiring autistic individuals to maintain eye contact. Research has since shown that forcing eye contact is not an effective solution. A better understanding of how face processing develops in the brain could help identify approaches that are more useful and appropriate.

Sources indicate that an ongoing challenge in autism research is separating neurological differences associated with autism itself from changes that may develop through the experience of living with the condition. According to the researchers, the patterns identified in this study suggest that differences in face processing are connected to underlying developmental characteristics of autism rather than simply reflecting accumulated life experiences.

"When we're seeing this expected refinement and specialization in non-autistic people, we're seeing a reduced developmental change in autistic people," McPartland explains.

Because the differences appear during development, the findings also raise the possibility that support aimed at helping autistic children interpret facial emotions could be particularly beneficial when introduced earlier in childhood.

Industry observers note that however, the researchers emphasize that autism does not necessarily create difficulties that require intervention. Many neurodivergent people experience little or no impairment related to their autism and may neither need nor want additional support. For others, challenges with recognizing faces or understanding facial expressions can complicate everyday social interactions.

Industry observers note that "Imagine navigating life when it's hard for you to perceive the information in another person's face, from navigating a playground to navigating a job interview," McPartland notes. "This is one of the critical areas that causes difficulty for many autistic people.".

Upcoming Brain Signals Could Help Improve Autism Diagnosis.

In a recent development, another potential application involves the search for more objective ways to assess autism. Currently, clinicians diagnose autism primarily by evaluating behavior because reliable biological tests are not yet available for routine diagnosis.

Scientists are investigating several possible biomarkers, which are measurable biological characteristics that could improve diagnostic assessments or help distinguish different groups within the autism spectrum.

In a recent development, the newly identified patterns of face related brain activity could contribute to that effort. By examining how these neural signals differ among individuals, researchers may eventually develop additional diagnostic tools or better identify autistic people who are likely to benefit from particular forms of support, including social skills therapy.

Although more research is necessary before these findings can be used in clinical practice, the study provides a new way to investigate how the autistic brain processes faces and how those responses change throughout childhood.

"This is a first step in introducing a new biomarker," McPartland notes.

#46133. Brain’s Insula Shapes Pain, Emotion, and the Placebo Effect
